title: From counts to chances
objectives: Turn counts into probabilities when every outcome is equally likely.
Count choices from several groups by multiplying the choices from each group.
Count top and bottom of a chance the same way.

screens.title: From counts to chances
screens.prose: When every outcome is equally likely, a chance is a count of what we want over a count of everything. The counting tools you have built do the work.
A fund picks 2 of 5 stocks, A to E, at random. Each cell above the diagonal is one pair, and all 10 pairs are equally likely.
screens.question: What is the chance the fund picks both A and B?

options.why: You counted $5 \times 4 = 20$ ordered picks on the bottom of the fraction but only AB on top. BA is the same pair.
That is the chance A is picked. B must be picked as well.
You used all 25 cells. A stock cannot pair with itself, and BA is the same pair as AB.

hints.text: How many pairs are there, and how many of them are AB?
This cell is the pair AB.
One pair out of 10 equally likely pairs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pairs above the diagonal, then the ones that are A with B.

explain.text: The grid holds 10 equally likely pairs, and exactly one of them is AB. So the chance is $\tfrac{1}{10}$.

screens.prose: Same fund, same 10 pairs. Tap a cell to select it, and tap it again to clear it.
screens.question: Tap every pair that contains stock C.

hints.text: C can be the first letter of a pair or the second.
C's row holds CD and CE.

feedback.correct: Four pairs contain C: AC, BC, CD and CE.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for C in both letters of each pair.

byKey.row-only: You found C's row. Pairs with C also sit in its column: AC and BC.
byKey.col-only: You found C's column. C's row holds CD and CE too.

explain.text: Four of the 10 pairs contain C, so $P(\text{C picked}) = \tfrac{4}{10} = \tfrac{2}{5}$. A quicker count: C's partner is any of the other 4.

screens.prose: You just used the rule for **equally likely outcomes**: $$P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{outcomes in the event}}{\text{all outcomes}}$$
screens.question: What is the chance the fund picks neither A nor B? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of neither A nor B

hints.text: Which stocks are left if A and B are both out?
These pairs use only C, D and E.
3 pairs out of 10.

feedback.correct: CD, CE and DE: 3 of the 10 pairs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pairs made only from C, D and E.

byKey.at-least-one: That is the chance of at least one of A and B, the complement.
byKey.replace: You multiplied $\tfrac{3}{5} \times \tfrac{3}{5}$, as if the same stock could be picked twice.
byKey.singles: You found the chance one pick avoids A and B. Both picks must avoid them.

explain.text: Pairs with neither A nor B use only C, D and E: CD, CE and DE. That is 3 of 10, so the chance is $\tfrac{3}{10}$. Its complement, at least one of A and B, is $\tfrac{7}{10}$.

screens.prose: A portfolio holds 3 stocks chosen from 8 and 2 bonds chosen from 5. Order does not matter inside either group.
screens.question: How many different portfolios are there?

hints.text: Choose the stocks, then the bonds. Do the two choices add or multiply?
There are $\binom{8}{3} = 56$ ways to choose the stocks.
$\binom{8}{3} \times \binom{5}{2} = 56 \times 10$.

feedback.correct: Each of the 56 stock choices goes with each of the 10 bond choices.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the stock choices and the bond choices, then combine them.

byKey.added: You added 56 and 10. Every stock choice goes with every bond choice, so they multiply.
byKey.pooled: You chose 5 from all 13 securities. That allows 4 stocks and 1 bond, which this portfolio does not.
byKey.ordered: You counted ordered picks, $8 \times 7 \times 6$ and $5 \times 4$. Order does not matter in a portfolio.

explain.text: There are $\binom{8}{3} = 56$ stock choices and $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ bond choices. Each goes with each, so by the product rule there are $56 \times 10 = 560$ portfolios.

screens.prose: An analyst builds one of the 560 portfolios at random, each equally likely. Stock S1 is her favourite.
screens.question: What is the chance S1 is in the portfolio? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Count the portfolios that contain S1.
With S1 in, choose the other 2 stocks from the other 7.
$\binom{7}{2} \times \binom{5}{2} = 21 \times 10 = 210$, out of 560.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix S1 in, count the ways to fill the rest, then divide by 560.

byKey.one-pick: That is the chance S1 is one particular pick. Three stocks are picked, so S1 has three chances.
byKey.one-portfolio: That is the chance of one particular portfolio. Many portfolios contain S1.
byKey.half: S1 is in or out, but those two cases are not equally likely.

explain.text: Portfolios with S1: $\binom{7}{2} \times 10 = 210$. So the chance is $\tfrac{210}{560} = \tfrac{3}{8}$. That matches the quick view: 3 of the 8 stocks are picked.

screens.prose: Back to the grid routes from the lesson on repeats: 3 steps right and 2 up, 10 routes in all. Pick one route at random, each equally likely.
screens.question: What is the chance the route passes through the marked cell? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Split each route at the marked cell.
Count routes from Start to this cell, then from it to End.
$2 \times 3 = 6$ routes pass through it, out of 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the routes that reach the cell, and the routes on from it to End.

byKey.added: You added the 2 ways in and the 3 ways out. Each way in goes with each way out, so they multiply.
byKey.cell: That treats the cell as one of 12 equally likely cells. It is the routes that are equally likely.
byKey.to-only: You counted the 2 ways to reach the cell. Each one carries on to End in 3 ways.
byKey.from-only: You counted the 3 ways from the cell to End. There are 2 ways to reach it first.

explain.text: Reaching the cell takes 1 R and 1 U: 2 ways. Leaving it takes 2 Rs and 1 U: 3 ways. By the product rule $2 \times 3 = 6$ of the 10 routes pass through, so the chance is $\tfrac{6}{10} = \tfrac{3}{5}$.

screens.prose: The fund again picks 2 of 5 stocks. A, B and C are tech stocks. Sam counts tech picks as $3 \times 2 = 6$, first pick then second, and divides by the 10 pairs.
screens.question: What is the chance both picks are tech stocks?

options.why: That is Sam's answer. $3 \times 2$ counts AB and BA separately, but the 10 pairs count each pair once.
You let the same stock be picked twice: $3 \times 3$ out of $5 \times 5$.
That is the chance the first pick alone is tech.

hints.text: Is $3 \times 2$ counting pairs or ordered picks?
These cells are the tech pairs.
Count the tech pairs in the grid, the same way the 10 were counted.

feedback.correct: Three tech pairs, AB, AC and BC, out of 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the top and the bottom the same way.

byKey.sam: You took Sam's count. $3 \times 2 = 6$ counts each tech pair twice, once per order, but the 10 counts each pair once. Count both the same way.

explain.text: The tech pairs are AB, AC and BC: 3 of the 10. Sam's 6 counted each pair twice, once per order. Ordered over ordered also works: $\tfrac{6}{20} = \tfrac{3}{10}$.

screens.prose: Why do ordered and unordered counts give the same chance when top and bottom agree? Pick $k$ items from $n$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Each unordered pick of $k$ items can be put in order in $k!$ ways.
So every ordered count is $k!$ times the unordered count: for the event, and for all outcomes.
$\dfrac{\text{ordered in event}}{\text{ordered in all}} = \dfrac{k! \times \text{unordered in event}}{k! \times \text{unordered in all}}$
The $k!$ cancels, so both ways give the same chance. Mixing them leaves a stray $k!$.

hints.text: Start with how one unordered pick becomes ordered picks.
The fraction needs the link between the two counts first.
Orders per pick, then the link for both counts, then the fraction, then cancel.

feedback.correct: The same $k!$ sits top and bottom, so it cancels.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Link the two kinds of count before you write the fraction.

byKey.cancel: Cancelling needs the fraction from the line before it, so it goes last.

explain.text: Each unordered pick gives $k!$ ordered picks, on top and on the bottom alike. The factor cancels, which is why $\tfrac{6}{20} = \tfrac{3}{10}$. Sam's $\tfrac{6}{10}$ kept a stray $2!$ on top.

screens.prose: A price starts at £100.00. At each of 4 steps it moves up £5.00 or down £5.00, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$, independently. Multiply along the branches, as on a tree diagram: each path has chance $(\tfrac{1}{2})^4 = \tfrac{1}{16}$. So all 16 paths are equally likely.

state.caption: Start £100.00. Each step: up £5.00 or down £5.00, chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each

screens.question: What is the chance the price ends at £100.00? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Ending at £100.00 needs how many ups and how many downs?
This path goes U, U, D, D and ends at £100.00.
Paths with 2 Us and 2 Ds: $\tfrac{4!}{2!\,2!} = 6$, out of $2^4 = 16$.

feedback.correct: 6 of the 16 equally likely paths end at £100.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the paths with two ups and two downs, then divide by 16.

byKey.end-prices: You treated the 5 end prices as equally likely. More paths lead to the middle prices, so count paths, not prices.
byKey.one-path: That is the chance of one particular path. Six different paths end at £100.00.
byKey.half: Ending level is not a coin toss. Count the paths that end there.
byKey.count: That is the number of paths. The chance divides it by all 16 paths.

explain.text: A path ends at £100.00 when it has 2 ups and 2 downs. There are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ such paths out of $2^4 = 16$, so the chance is $\tfrac{6}{16} = 0.375$. Pricing with trees adds up chances like this, path by path.

ideas: With equally likely outcomes, a chance is the count we want over the count of everything.
Count top and bottom the same way: both ordered or both unordered.
Choices from separate groups multiply. Routes through a point are routes to it times routes on from it.

formula.name: Equally likely outcomes
formula.note: Only when every outcome is equally likely. The paths of a fair tree are; its end prices are not.

summary.trap: Counting the top in order and the bottom without order makes the chance $k!$ times too big.

quiz.prose: Two cards are dealt from a standard 52-card deck. There are $\binom{52}{2} = 1326$ equally likely hands.
quiz.question: What is the chance both cards are hearts?

options.why: You used $\tfrac{1}{4} \times \tfrac{1}{4}$, as if the first card went back.
You counted $13 \times 12$ ordered heart picks over 1326 unordered hands. Count both the same way.
That is the chance one card is a heart.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the two-heart hands the same way as the 1326.

explain.text: Two-heart hands: $\binom{13}{2} = 78$. So the chance is $\tfrac{78}{1326} = \tfrac{1}{17}$.

quiz.prose: A risk committee takes 2 of 6 traders and 1 of 4 analysts.
quiz.question: How many different committees are possible?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose from each group, then multiply.

byKey.added: You added 15 and 4. Each pair of traders goes with each analyst, so they multiply.
byKey.pooled: You got 120. Either you picked 3 from all 10 people, or you counted the traders in order. Choose 2 of 6 without order, then 1 of 4.

explain.text: There are $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ ways to pick the traders and 4 ways to pick the analyst. So $15 \times 4 = 60$ committees.

quiz.prose: A price moves up or down at each of 5 steps, with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each way, independently.
quiz.question: What is the chance of exactly 2 up moves? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the paths with 2 Us and 3 Ds, then divide by $2^5$.

byKey.end-prices: You treated the 6 end prices as equally likely. Count paths instead.
byKey.one-path: That is one path. Ten paths have exactly 2 ups.
byKey.ups: You divided 2 ups by 5 steps. Count whole paths instead.

explain.text: Paths with 2 ups are arrangements of UUDDD: $\tfrac{5!}{2!\,3!} = 10$. All $2^5 = 32$ paths are equally likely, so the chance is $\tfrac{10}{32} = 0.3125$.

quiz.prose: On a grid, every route from Start to End takes 4 steps right and 2 steps up. One route is picked at random, each equally likely.
quiz.question: What is the chance its first step is to the right?

options.why: You treated right and up as a coin toss. More of the routes start with R, because there are more Rs.
That is the chance of one particular route.
You divided routes by steps. A chance is routes over routes.

feedback.correct: 10 of the 15 routes start with R.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the routes that start with R, then divide by all routes.

explain.text: All routes: $\binom{6}{2} = 15$. Routes starting with R leave 3 Rs and 2 Us: $\binom{5}{2} = 10$. So the chance is $\tfrac{10}{15} = \tfrac{2}{3}$, which is also 4 Rs out of 6 steps.
